title: Living ashtpadi 13

segments.voice: Yesterday, maleen, and your line: bless instead. Did a criticism turn into a good wish even once? Today we take the thirteenth ashtpadi out of the hymn and into an ordinary day. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

Try counting, just for one lunch break, how much of the talk around you is about people who aren't there. Who's dating whom. Who got the promotion and didn't deserve it. What the neighbor is doing with that yard. Most of it isn't cruel. It's just the easy, warm currency of being together. And that's what makes it hard: gossip isn't usually a decision. It's a habit of the tongue, running ahead of us. Sukhmani's thirteenth ashtpadi warned about slander of the holy. Living it means watching the smaller cousin, the one that shows up at lunch.
screen: `COUNT THE TALK AT LUNCH.` → `ABOUT PEOPLE WHO AREN'T THERE.` → `A HABIT OF THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Gurbani's word for the tongue is rasnaa, and it sits right beside ras: taste, juice, flavor. The tongue is the tasting organ, and the Gurus play with that. What the tongue keeps tasting, it gets a taste for. Hymns speak of a tongue that savors the Name, that has found the sweetest flavor and wants nothing else. The opposite is a tongue that has acquired a taste for other people's faults, and keeps going back for more. Guru Nanak puts it bluntly in Asa di Var, the hymn we met a few days ago: speaking harsh, tasteless words, the body and mind themselves become tasteless. The word is phikaa. Bland, flat, insipid, like food with no salt. It's a striking picture. Unkind talk doesn't just wound someone else; it drains the flavor out of the person talking. Put that beside the thirteenth ashtpadi and the shape is clear. Slander of the holy stains the mind. Everyday gossip, its small cousin, flattens it. Both start on the tongue. So why guard the tongue rather than the thoughts? Because the tongue is where a passing thought becomes a habit. A thought about someone's faults can drift by. Said out loud, it gets an audience, a laugh, a reply, and comes back stronger tomorrow. Guarding the tongue is like putting a gate at the end of a path: the thoughts may still wander up to it, but they don't get out into the world. And a gate is a small thing to build: one changed subject, at one lunch table.
screen: `RASNAA: THE TASTING TONGUE.` · `A TASTE FOR THE NAME, OR FOR FAULTS.` · `PHIKAA: HARSH WORDS MAKE YOU BLAND.` · `A GATE AT THE END OF THE PATH.` · then, large: `GUARD THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest the tongue. Close your mouth gently and let the tongue lie soft against the floor of your mouth, not pressing anywhere. Notice how much it wants to move, even in silence: the tiny shapes of words forming. Each time you feel it start to shape a word, let it go soft again. Two minutes of a quiet tongue. If you pray, you can let it hold one word only, Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Rasnaa, the tongue, the taster. It can learn a taste for the Name or for faults, and harsh words leave the speaker phikaa, flavorless.
Your line: guard the tongue. Try a whole day without gossip. When talk turns to someone who isn't there, change the subject, or say something good about them. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

screen: `DAY 489 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 14, SALOK: GIVE UP CLEVERNESS.`

howItsDone: Gurbani returns often to the rasnaa, the tongue, and to the sweetness of speaking the Name; Sukhmani's warnings on slander and Guru Nanak's line on harsh words are read as a guard on gossip.

pairs: where a thought becomes a habit

myth: Guru Nanak says harsh words leave the speaker's own body and mind flat
in Asa di Var, speaking phikaa words makes body and mind phikaa.
Gurbani's word for tongue has nothing to do with taste
rasnaa sits beside ras, taste, and the Gurus play on the pair.
this lesson treats gossip mainly as a deliberate decision
it calls gossip a habit of the tongue, running ahead of us.

fork.setup: at lunch, talk turns to a coworker who isn't there. you want to live ashtpadi 13. what's your move?
options: join in, but keep it mild.
change the subject, or say something good about them.
fork.reveal: guard the tongue: close the gate gently. a lecture just turns the gossip toward you, and joining in feeds the taste.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rasnaa, the tongue, the taster; Gurbani plays it against ras, taste.

trapdoor: what you thought: guard the tongue means don't swear.
what it means: the tongue grows a taste for what it keeps saying, so watch what you feed it.
what a scholar hears: Asa di Var's line phikai boliai tan man phikaa hoi turns a cooking word, flat and unsalted, into a word about the self.
